member.name: M:KeshavSingh.Localization.ApplicationBuilderExtensions.InitKeshavLocalizationAsync(System.IServiceProvider,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary:
Creates the indexes, applies every registered , and leaves all three caches loaded. Call once after app.Build() and before serving traffic.
Order is deliberate and load-bearing: the config registry first (it owns the URL/icon host allowlist that locale icons and config defaults are validated against), then the locales (they define the default language every other step resolves against), then the strings (seeds for an unregistered locale are skipped, so the locales must exist first).
Seeding is additive at every level — nothing here can overwrite an editor's change — and is skipped entirely when Localization:SeedOnStartup is false.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Localization.ConfigRegistryService
member.summary:
The runtime config registry: a typed key/value store (collection config_entries) that lets URLs, icons, labels, limits and feature flags be changed by an Admin without a redeploy, so no app has to hard-code them.
Three things make this safe to expose at all:
Every value is validated by declared type on write () — URLs and icons against a host allowlist, because they are rendered into public pages.
Exposure is decided per entry by , and the public projection is built by filtering on it here — a caller can never ask for a wider scope.
Secret entries are AES-encrypted at rest and write-only: no endpoint returns their value, only whether one is set.
The whole registry is cached in memory (it is read on nearly every request) and re-read on every write. changes with the cache so clients know when to refresh.

member.name: M:KeshavSingh.Localization.ConfigRegistryService.SeedSystemEntriesAsync(System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary:
Registers the config keys declared by the host app's s, so every key a client reads exists with the value the code used to hard-code. Seeding therefore changes no behaviour on first run — it only makes the value editable.
Additive: an existing row's value, default and description are left alone, so a deployment can never undo an admin's edit. What IS reasserted is the contract: the seeded entries are re-marked IsSystem (editable, not deletable) and their declared type and scope are re-applied, because other apps read those as a promise. A previous version's system entry that no seed declares any more loses the flag and becomes deletable.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Localization.ConfigValueValidator
member.summary:
Validates every runtime-configurable value at the trust boundary, by declared type. Allow-lists only — an unrecognised type, scheme, host or shape is rejected rather than sanitised.
Why this is strict: these values are edited at runtime and a good number of them are served to anonymous visitors and rendered into a page (icons, logo URLs, colours, links). Without this, the config registry would be a stored-XSS and open-redirect surface with an admin-sized blast radius. Values are stored canonicalised so the client never has to re-parse them.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Localization.Controllers.LocalizationController
member.summary:
The localisation surface. Two audiences, deliberately separated:
Public (anonymous) — GET /api/i18n/manifest, /locales and /bundle/{locale}. This is how every site gets its text at runtime instead of compiling it in. Responses carry an ETag derived from the content, so a client that polls pays for a 304 and nothing else. Only ENABLED locales and only the namespaces asked for are ever returned — the admin app's strings are not reachable from a public page.
Editorial (Editor/Admin) — everything under /api/i18n/admin: the grid, bulk save, import, export and cache refresh. Nothing here is anonymous, and no endpoint returns anything an editor could not already see on the screen.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Localization.TranslationFormats
member.summary:
The interchange formats the catalogue can be exported to and imported from, in one place so the API, the UI and the docs cannot disagree about what is supported.
json — flat keys ("blog.nav.home": "Home"). Import and export.
nested — nested objects, what most i18n tooling expects. Export only as a distinct name; on import nested and flat JSON are both accepted as json.
csv — namespace,key,value[,notes] with a header row. Import and export.
xlsx — a workbook, one sheet per namespace, with the source language alongside. Import and export. The format to hand a non-technical translator.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Localization.TranslationService
member.summary:
The translation catalogue (collection translations) and the bundles built from it.
How a client uses it: fetch GET /api/i18n/manifest (which locales exist, and a version per locale), then GET /api/i18n/bundle/{locale} for the flat namespace.key → value map. Missing strings are filled in from the locale's fallback chain, so a half-translated language still renders. Nothing is compiled into any app's build.
The catalogue is held in memory and rebuilt on every write: it is read by every public page load, and it is small (thousands of short strings at most). Bundles are memoised per locale+namespace-set and dropped whenever the catalogue changes.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Localization.TranslationWorkbook
member.summary:
The .xlsx side of import/export — the format to hand someone who translates in a spreadsheet rather than in a JSON file.
Layout: one sheet per namespace, columns Key | Source | Translation | Notes, header frozen. The Source column is the default language's text and is read-only guidance; only Translation (and optionally Notes) is read back on import, matched by the Key column and the sheet name. That means an exported file round-trips unedited, and a translator can fill in blanks without understanding the key syntax.
Columns are located by header name, not position, so a translator who inserts a comment column or reorders things does not break the import.
